opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what the gap actually is, because people often treat "sim-to-real" as one problem when it's really several stacked on top of each other.

There's the visual gap: lighting, textures, reflections, sensor noise. That's the part that's improved the most, especially with better rendering and generative models. Then there's the physics gap: contact, friction, deformable objects, cables, cloth, liquids. That's much harder, because small errors in contact dynamics compound very quickly in manipulation. And then there's what I'd call the distribution gap: the tasks, layouts, and messiness of real homes and factories are just different from what engineers think to put in a simulator. That last one gets underestimated a lot.

So for a synthetic-data company, I don't think the answer is "make the simulator perfectly realistic." That's a very expensive road with diminishing returns. A few things matter more in practice.

First, treat real data as the anchor, not the competitor. The most effective setups I've seen use a relatively small amount of high-quality real data, often teleoperation, to define what "correct" looks like, and then use synthetic data to expand coverage around it: more object variations, more viewpoints, more failure and recovery cases. Synthetic data is very good at breadth. Real data is very good at grounding.

Second, randomize deliberately rather than blindly. Domain randomization works, but if you randomize everything you can end up teaching the model that the world is far noisier than it really is. The better approach is to measure where your policy fails in the real world and focus variation there. It becomes a closed loop: deploy, find the failure modes, generate targeted data, retrain.

Third, be really rigorous about evaluation. A synthetic-data company's value proposition has to be proven on real robots, on real tasks, with clear metrics, not on benchmarks inside its own simulator. If customers can't see that adding your data improves real-world success rates per dollar compared with just collecting more teleop data, then the business doesn't really hold up.

And fourth, I think the line between "synthetic" and "real" is blurring. With world models and video generation, you can take real captures and augment them, or generate scenes conditioned on real environments. That kind of hybrid, real-to-sim-to-real, is probably where a lot of the progress will come from, rather than pure simulation built from scratch.

So my short answer is: don't try to win by replacing real data. Win by making each piece of real data go ten times further, and prove it on hardware.

r001.rationale: The response describes several components of the gap and ways synthetic data can help, but does not frame the question as how large the gap can be while synthetic data remains useful.

r002.rationale: The response says companies should prove their data improves real-world results, but does not state that a company cannot identify the gap if clients handle model training.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest that the gap is not one thing. There are at least three different gaps, and companies tend to collapse them.

The first is the visual gap. Rendering doesn't look like a real camera. That one gets the most attention, and frankly it's the most solved. Domain randomization, better renderers, neural rendering on top of real scans. If a team tells me their main problem in 2026 is that the images don't look real enough, I get a little suspicious.

The second is the physics gap, and this is the one that actually kills robotics projects. Contact, friction, deformable objects, cables, cloth, liquids. A simulator will let a gripper close on a plastic bag and the bag behaves like a rigid block. The policy learns something that is simply false about the world. No amount of visual realism fixes that, because the error is in the dynamics, not the pixels.

The third gap is the one nobody likes to talk about, which is the distribution gap. Even if your simulator were perfect, someone had to decide what scenes to generate. Which objects, which clutter, which lighting, which failure modes. That person's imagination becomes the ceiling for the robot. Real data is messy in ways you didn't think to ask for.

So how should a synthetic-data company address this? A few things I'd push for.

One, stop selling synthetic data as a replacement and start selling it as an amplifier. The healthiest setups I've seen use a small amount of real data as the anchor and synthetic data to fill in the long tail around it. Real-to-sim, not just sim-to-real. You scan the actual warehouse, you capture the actual objects, and then you perturb from there. The real data tells you where the distribution actually lives.

Two, measure the gap instead of asserting you've closed it. Most companies show you a nice video. Very few can tell you, quantitatively, how performance degrades when you move from their sim to a real cell, and on which tasks. If I were running one of these companies, I'd publish that number for every release, even when it's embarrassing. Customers are going to find out anyway.

Three, invest in physics over pixels. The team that ships a genuinely good deformable-body model, or realistic sensor noise for depth cameras, is going to be more valuable than the team with the prettiest renders. It's less glamorous and harder to demo, which is exactly why it's underinvested.

And four, build the feedback loop into the product. When a robot fails in deployment, that failure should flow back and become a new synthetic scenario within days. The gap isn't a static thing you close once. It's something you keep chasing, and the companies that win will be the ones with the shortest loop between a real-world surprise and an updated training set.

The uncomfortable truth is that a synthetic-data company that does this well ends up being partly a real-data company too. I think the ones that resist that are going to struggle.

r001.rationale: The response describes several kinds of gap and recommends using synthetic data to amplify real data, but does not frame the issue as how large the gap can be while synthetic data remains useful.

r002.rationale: The response urges companies to measure and publish sim-to-real performance degradation, but does not say they cannot identify the gap when clients handle model training.

astra-6.text:
I think synthetic-data companies should start with a specific robot task and work backward from what fails in the real world. The gap isn’t just whether an image looks realistic. It can be friction, contact forces, sensor noise, latency, or how an object deforms when you grasp it. A simulation can look convincing and still teach the robot the wrong behavior.

So you need a tight feedback loop: collect some real-world data, identify where the policy fails, use those failures to improve the simulation and generate targeted examples, then test again on the robot. Domain randomization helps, but the ranges need to reflect plausible conditions. Otherwise, you’re adding variation without necessarily adding useful coverage.

And I’d measure success by improvement on real tasks, rather than the volume of synthetic data produced. Does the robot grasp more reliably? Does it recover when an object slips? Does it work under conditions it hasn’t seen? That’s ultimately what customers are buying. Synthetic data is most valuable when it makes that real-world learning loop faster and less expensive.

r001.rationale: It discusses closing the synthetic-to-real gap and says synthetic data is useful when it improves real-world tasks, but it does not frame the central question as how large the gap can be while the data remains useful.

r002.rationale: It recommends a feedback loop involving real-world testing, but does not state that a company supplying data alone cannot identify the gap when clients handle model training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think synthetic-data companies should treat that gap as something to measure continuously. A simulation can look convincing and still teach a robot the wrong behavior, because friction, contact, sensor noise, or timing differs from the real world.

So I’d start with a specific task and a small, representative set of real-world trials. Where does the robot fail? Is it perception, grasping, or recovery after a mistake? Then use those failures to decide what to improve in the simulator and what synthetic examples to generate.

Randomizing conditions helps, but the variation needs to reflect what the robot will actually encounter. And some things will still require real data, especially contact-rich interactions.

Ultimately, the product shouldn’t be judged by how realistic the images look or how many samples it generates. It should be judged by whether it improves success rates on real robots, including under conditions the system hasn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: The response recommends measuring and reducing the gap and judging synthetic data by real-robot success, but does not frame the question as how large the gap can be while synthetic data remains useful.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a company supplying only data cannot identify the gap when clients handle model training.
